recall.minute: Approximate control represents q̂(s, a, θ) = θᵀφ(s, a) and applies semi-gradient updates on the features of the pair taken. In the dino example (θ = [1.0, 0.5, 1.0], θ′ = [0.1, 0.3, 1.0], γ = 0.2, α = 0.9, r = 2, φ(S1,0) = [1,0,0], q̂(S2,0) = 1.5, q̂(S2,1) = 2.5), SARSA's target 2.30 gives θ₁ = 2.17, Q-learning's 2.50 gives 2.35, and Double Q (select with θ, evaluate with θ′: 1.40) gives 2.28 and 2.152; the honest target with true next values 2.0 is 2.40, so the max overestimates. Q-learning with approximation has all three deadly-triad ingredients. DQN adds experience replay (random mini-batches from a buffer, breaking correlation and reusing data; prioritised replay favours high TD error) and a target network θ⁻ synced every C steps; Double DQN selects with the online network and evaluates with θ⁻. In a tiny NumPy experiment both DQN and naive online Q-learning found the goal, but the naive learner's values exploded to ~10⁵.
